grammarPoints.title: 이에요/예요
grammarPoints.description: Use this ending when saying that a person or thing is a noun: 'I am a student' or 'That is a book'. It is polite but everyday speech.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Start with the noun, not the whole sentence. If its final syllable has a bottom consonant, attach 이에요; otherwise attach 예요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 학생이에요. — I am a student. 학생 ends in ㄴ, so 학생 + 이에요 = 학생이에요. 의사 ends in a vowel, so 의사 + 예요 = 의사예요.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not use 예요 after 학생, or write 이예요. The negative version is the separate construction N이/가 아니에요.

notes.title: Consonant vs Vowel
notes.content: Use 이에요 after consonant-ending nouns (학생이에요) and 예요 after vowel-ending nouns (의사예요).

notes.title: Contracted Form
notes.content: 이예요 is a common misspelling. Write 이에요 after a final consonant and 예요 after a vowel; 아니에요 is a separate correct form.

lessonExamples.notes: 책 ends in ㄱ, so use 이에요. Compare 의자예요, where 의자 ends in a vowel. The negative copula is 아니에요.

grammarPoints.title: N이/가 아니다 (아니에요)
grammarPoints.description: Use this pattern to say a person or thing is NOT a noun: 'I'm not a student' or 'It isn't coffee'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Say the noun being denied, add 이 after a final consonant or 가 after a vowel, and finish with 아니에요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 학생이 아니에요. — I'm not a student. 학생 ends in a consonant: 학생 + 이 + 아니에요 = 학생이 아니에요. 의사 ends in a vowel: 의사가 아니에요.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 아니에요 is the correct spelling, not 아니예요. 안 학생이에요 is not the normal way to negate a noun.

notes.title: Compare
notes.content: 학생이에요 (I am a student) → 학생이 아니에요 (I am not a student). 의사예요 → 의사가 아니에요.

notes.title: Not 안
notes.content: Do not put 안 before a noun to make a negative copula. Use 아니에요 for noun identification.

grammarPoints.title: 은/는
grammarPoints.description: 은/는 tells the listener what you're talking about. It often marks a topic or sets up a contrast: 'As for me...'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 은 after a noun ending in a consonant; add 는 after a vowel-ending noun.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 저는 학생이에요. — As for me, I am a student. 저 has no final consonant, so 저 + 는 = 저는. 저는 학생이에요 gives information about the topic 'me'.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: It is not interchangeable with 이/가 in every context. In 'Who is the student?', the answer commonly uses 이/가 to identify the person.

notes.title: Consonant vs Vowel
notes.content: Use 은 after consonant-ending nouns (이름은) and 는 after vowel-ending nouns (저는).

notes.title: Topic vs Subject
notes.content: The topic particle marks "what we're talking about." The subject particle 이/가 (Lesson 2) marks "who/what does the action." They overlap but aren't the same.

lessonExamples.englishHint: As for me, I am a student.
lessonExamples.notes: Uses 이에요/예요 (GP1). 저 ends in vowel → 는.

lessonExamples.englishHint: As for the name, it's Minsu.
lessonExamples.notes: Uses 예요 (GP1). 이름 ends in consonant ㅁ → 은.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I am a student. Minsu is a doctor.
lessonExamples.notes: 는 can mark contrasting topics; both clauses use only previously introduced grammar.

cards.englishHint: Today is Monday. Tomorrow is Tuesday.

grammarPoints.title: 이것
grammarPoints.description: 이것 means 'this thing' near the speaker. It belongs to the 이것/그것/저것 pointing system.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Choose 이것 for something close to you. Add the necessary sentence particle AFTER the complete word, such as 이것은.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 이것은 책이에요. — This is a book. 이것은 책이에요: identify the nearby thing as a book. The topic particle 은 follows the final consonant ㅅ in 이것.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 이거 is a common casual form, but 이거은 is wrong. You would say 이거는 or 이것은; the remaining particle matters.

notes.title: Casual Form
notes.content: 이것 → 이거 in casual speech. Both are correct.

notes.title: Three-Way System
notes.content: Korean has three demonstratives based on distance: 이 (near speaker), 그 (near listener), 저 (far from both).

lessonExamples.notes: Uses 은/는 (GP3), 이에요/예요 (GP1).

grammarPoints.title: 그것
grammarPoints.description: 그것 means 'that thing' near the listener or already mentioned. It contrasts with 이것 (here) and 저것 (over there).

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Choose 그것 when the item is by the other person or in the shared conversation. Then attach the right particle: 그것은.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 그것은 연필이에요. — That is a pencil. 그것은 연필이에요 points to the other person's item (or a previously mentioned item) and calls it a pencil.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 그것 does not always mean 'far away'; 저것 is for something away from both speakers. Casual 그거 needs its own correct particle.

notes.title: Casual Form
notes.content: 그것 → 그거 in casual speech.

notes.title: Referencing Earlier Topics
notes.content: 그것 can also refer to something previously mentioned in conversation, like English "that" or "it."

grammarPoints.title: 저것
grammarPoints.description: 저것 means 'that thing over there', away from both the speaker and listener.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Use 저것 for a visible item at a distance, then add a particle as needed.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 저것은 학교예요. — That over there is a school. 저것은 학교예요 describes a building over there as a school. 저것 ends in ㅅ, so add 은.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not confuse 저것 (away from both people) with 그것 (by the listener or already mentioned). 저거은 is not grammatical.

notes.title: Casual Form
notes.content: 저것 → 저거 in casual speech.

notes.title: Don't Confuse
notes.content: 저것 (that over there) is different from 저 (I, humble). Context makes it clear.

lessonExamples.englishHint: That over there is a school.
That over there is a mountain.

cards.englishHint: That over there is a school.
That over there is a hospital.

grammarPoints.title: 의
grammarPoints.description: 의 links one noun to another to show ownership or a relationship: 'someone's book'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Put the owner first, then 의, then the owned noun: 민수 + 의 + 책.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 저의 이름은 민수예요. — My name is Minsu. 저의 이름은 민수예요: 저의 means 'my'; 이름 is the thing being described. Spoken 저의 often becomes 제.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 의 does not simply replace English 'of' in every phrase. Pronunciation may sound like 에, but the written particle is 의.

notes.title: Pronunciation
notes.content: Though written 의, it is often pronounced 에 in casual speech.

notes.title: Contractions
notes.content: 저의 → 제 (my, polite), 나의 → 내 (my, casual). These contracted forms are very common.

lessonExamples.notes: Uses 은/는 (GP3), 예요 (GP1).
Uses 이것 (GP4), 은/는 (GP3), 이에요 (GP1).

grammarPoints.title: 도
grammarPoints.description: 도 means 'also' or 'too'. It adds a person or thing to something already true.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 도 directly to the noun or pronoun being added: 저 + 도 = 저도.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 저도 학생이에요. — I am also a student. 저도 학생이에요 means 'I am a student too'. 도 tells the listener someone else is a student as well.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 도 often replaces 은/는 or 이/가 on the same noun; do not stack 저도는 as a normal topic expression.

notes.title: Replaces Other Particles
notes.content: 도 replaces 은/는, 이/가, or 을/를 — don't stack them (✗ 저는도, ✓ 저도).

notes.title: Position Matters
notes.content: 도 attaches to the noun it modifies: 저도 학생이에요 = "I am also a student" (emphasis on "I"), 학생도 = "a student too."

lessonExamples.notes: Uses 이에요 (GP1). N+1 OK: only uses GPs 1–8.
Uses 이것 (GP4), 의 (GP7), 이에요 (GP1).

grammarPoints.title: 이다
grammarPoints.description: 이다 is the dictionary form used to link a noun with 'is/am/are'. You will mostly speak with endings such as 이에요/예요.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: In plain dictionary-style sentences, attach 이다 to a noun: 학생 + 이다.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 학생이다. — He is a student. 학생이다 is a plain statement. In a normal polite exchange, use 학생이에요 instead.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 이다 is not the normal way to end a polite conversation. It also attaches to nouns, not arbitrary action-verb stems.

notes.title: Base Form
notes.content: 이다 is the base form you'll find in dictionaries. In conversation, use its conjugated forms (이에요/예요 or 입니다).

notes.title: No Space
notes.content: 이다 attaches directly to the noun with no space: 학생이다, not 학생 이다.

grammarPoints.title: 이/가
grammarPoints.description: 이/가 identifies who or what is doing something, or what exists. It is often especially useful when answering 'who?' or 'what?'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: First identify who or what the sentence is about. Add 이 after a noun with a final consonant, or 가 after a noun ending in a vowel.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 이름이 민수예요. — The name is Minsu. 이름이 민수예요: 이름 ends with ㅁ, so take 이. 민수가 학생이에요 identifies Minsu as the student.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 은/는 sets a topic or contrast; 이/가 marks a subject. Sometimes both work but change what the listener focuses on.

notes.title: Consonant vs Vowel
notes.content: Use 이 after consonant-ending nouns (물이) and 가 after vowel-ending nouns (날씨가).

notes.title: Subject vs Topic
notes.content: 이/가 marks new or emphasized information ("Who came?" → 민수가 왔어요). 은/는 marks the general topic ("As for Minsu, he came").

lessonExamples.notes: 날씨 ends in vowel → 가. Uses vocab 좋아요 (good).
물 ends in consonant ㄹ → 이.

lessonExamples.englishHint: Who is a student? Minsu is a student.
lessonExamples.notes: 가 identifies the subject; use a copula here, before verb endings are introduced.

cards.englishHint: That over there is a cat.
Who is the teacher? Minsu is the teacher.

grammarPoints.title: 있다/있어요
grammarPoints.description: 있어요 means someone or something exists, is somewhere, or is possessed. Context tells you which sense is intended.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Put the thing that exists before 있어요, usually with 이/가. For a location use 에: 책이 집에 있어요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 고양이가 있어요. — There is a cat. 고양이가 있어요 means 'There is a cat' or 'I have a cat', depending on context. 가 marks the cat as the thing present.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 있어요 is not a general equivalent of English 'is'. For 'is a student', use 학생이에요; use 있어요 for existence, location or possession.

notes.title: Three Meanings
notes.content: Existence: 의자가 있어요 (there is a chair). Possession: 돈이 있어요 (I have money). Location: 여기에 있어요 (I am here).

notes.title: Subject Particle
notes.content: 이/가 introduces what exists: 고양이가 있어요 (there is a cat). 은/는 is possible when making it the topic or contrasting it: 고양이는 있어요 (as for a cat, there is one).

cards.englishHint: There is a book in the bag.

grammarPoints.title: 없다/없어요
grammarPoints.hint: to not exist, to not have
grammarPoints.description: 없어요 says that something doesn't exist, isn't present, or isn't possessed.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Name what is missing and add 없어요, usually after its 이/가-marked noun.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 시간이 없어요. — I don't have time. 시간이 없어요: 시간이 is 'time' as the thing missing; 없어요 means it is not available.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 없어요 is not the negative of 'I am a student'. Use 학생이 아니에요 for noun identity; 없어요 is for absence.

notes.title: Pair with 있다
notes.content: 있다 (have/exist) ↔ 없다 (don't have / doesn't exist). They are a pair, not verb + negation.

notes.title: Not 안 있다
notes.content: For absence or lack of possession, use 없어요: 돈이 없어요 (I don’t have money). Learn it as the usual opposite of 있어요 in these examples.

grammarPoints.title: -아요/어요
grammarPoints.description: This is the basic polite ending for everyday actions and descriptions, like 'eat', 'go', or 'is good'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Remove 다 from the dictionary form. With many regular verbs, use 아요 after a last stem vowel ㅏ/ㅗ and 어요 otherwise; 하다 becomes 해요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 저는 공부해요. — I study. 공부하다 → 공부하 + 여요 → 공부해요. 저는 공부해요 is 'I study' in everyday polite speech.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Many verbs contract: 가다 → 가요, 보다 → 봐요. Irregular verbs need extra rules; don't mechanically paste 아요/어요 onto every spelling.

notes.title: Vowel Harmony
notes.content: Regular stems usually take -아요 after ㅏ or ㅗ and -어요 after other vowels. 하다 → 해요; contractions and irregulars need separate attention.

notes.title: Examples
notes.content: 가다 → 가요 (go), 먹다 → 먹어요 (eat), 공부하다 → 공부해요 (study).

lessonExamples.notes: Uses 은/는 (GP3), 을/를 (GP10). 공부하다 → 공부해요.
Uses 은/는 (GP3), 을/를 (GP10). 먹다 → 먹어요 (stem 먹 has ㅓ vowel).
가다 → 가요 (stem 가 has ㅏ vowel → 아요 contracts to 가요).
보다 → 봐요. The stem 보 and 아 combine to make 봐.

grammarPoints.title: ㅂ irregular: 춥다 → 추워요
grammarPoints.hint: Some descriptive and action verbs ending in ㅂ change that final consonant when a vowel-starting ending follows.
grammarPoints.description: Some descriptive and action verbs ending in ㅂ change that final consonant when a vowel-starting ending follows. This is a common pronunciation and spelling pattern, not a new tense.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: For a ㅂ-irregular stem, remove 다, drop final ㅂ and add 우 before -어: 춥다

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: For a ㅂ-irregular stem, remove 다, drop final ㅂ and add 우 before -어: 춥다 → 추워요. In 돕다 and 곱다, the resulting vowel can be 오 (도와요).

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 오늘 날씨가 추워요. — The weather is cold today. The final ㅂ in 춥다 changes before the polite vowel ending, giving 추워요 rather than 춥어요.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Not every ㅂ-final verb is irregular: 입다 → 입어요 and 잡다 → 잡아요 remain regular. Learn exceptions with the vocabulary entry.

grammarPoints.title: ㄷ irregular: 듣다 → 들어요
grammarPoints.hint: Certain verbs whose stems end in ㄷ change it to ㄹ when followed by a vowel-starting ending.
grammarPoints.description: Certain verbs whose stems end in ㄷ change it to ㄹ when followed by a vowel-starting ending. The action stays the same; the stem spelling changes.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: Remove 다 from selected ㄷ verbs and change ㄷ to ㄹ before vowel endings: 듣다

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Remove 다 from selected ㄷ verbs and change ㄷ to ㄹ before vowel endings: 듣다 → 들어요, 걷다 → 걸어요. With consonant endings, ㄷ remains (듣습니다).

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 음악을 들어요. — I listen to music. The stem 듣- becomes 들- before 어요, so the polite present form is 들어요 rather than 듣어요.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Not every ㄷ-final verb changes. 받다 → 받아요 and 닫다 → 닫아요 are regular; only certain verbs such as 듣다 and 걷다 change.

grammarPoints.title: 르 irregular: 모르다 → 몰라요
grammarPoints.hint: Many stems ending in 르 change before 아요 or 어요, adding ㄹ to the preceding syllable.
grammarPoints.description: Many stems ending in 르 change before 아요 or 어요, adding ㄹ to the preceding syllable. This is why 'don't know' takes the form 몰라요.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: Remove 다. For a 르-irregular stem, remove ㅡ from 르 and add ㄹ as the preceding syllable's final consonant; then choose 라/러: 모르다

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Remove 다. For a 르-irregular stem, remove ㅡ from 르 and add ㄹ as the preceding syllable's final consonant; then choose 라/러: 모르다 → 몰라요; 부르다 → 불러요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 저는 그 사람을 몰라요. — I don't know that person. 모르다 produces 몰라요 because the preceding syllable gains ㄹ and 르 becomes 라 before the polite ending.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not treat every 르 verb as identical. 따르다 → 따라요 does not use the doubling rule; the rule is lexical and needs examples.

grammarPoints.title: 으 deletion: 쓰다 → 써요
grammarPoints.hint: A verb or descriptive verb whose stem ends in ㅡ often loses that vowel when an 아/어 ending is attached.
grammarPoints.description: A verb or descriptive verb whose stem ends in ㅡ often loses that vowel when an 아/어 ending is attached. The preceding vowel helps determine the new form.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: Remove 다; remove stem-final ㅡ before 아요/어요, then check the preceding vowel: 쓰다

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Remove 다; remove stem-final ㅡ before 아요/어요, then check the preceding vowel: 쓰다 → 써요, 바쁘다 → 바빠요, 예쁘다 → 예뻐요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 편지를 써요. — I write a letter. 쓰다 has only a stem-final ㅡ to drop, so it combines with 어요 as 써요, not 쓰어요.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: This is different from the 르 irregular doubling pattern. 쓰다 → 써요 has no extra ㄹ; 모르다 → 몰라요 does.

grammarPoints.title: 해체: -아/-어 (casual speech)
grammarPoints.hint: In relaxed conversations with close friends or younger people, Korean often uses the same everyday ending without 요.
grammarPoints.description: In relaxed conversations with close friends or younger people, Korean often uses the same everyday ending without 요. Choosing this form depends on the relationship, not simply the sentence's meaning.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: Make the same present form as -아요/-어요, then remove the polite 요: 가요

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Make the same present form as -아요/-어요, then remove the polite 요: 가요 → 가, 먹어요 → 먹어, 공부해요 → 공부해.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 친구야, 지금 가. — Hey, friend, I'm leaving now. 친구한테 '지금 가'라고 말해요: 가 is the casual form of 가요 used with someone close to the speaker.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not use casual speech automatically with strangers, teachers or customers. The meaning stays similar but the social effect can be inappropriate.

grammarPoints.title: 을/를
grammarPoints.description: 을/를 marks the thing directly affected by an action: what you eat, read, buy, or watch.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 을 if the noun ends in a final consonant; add 를 if it ends in a vowel.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 커피를 마셔요. — I drink coffee. 커피 ends in a vowel, so 커피 + 를 = 커피를. 커피를 마셔요 = 'I drink coffee'.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't mark the person doing an action with 을/를; use 이/가 or a topic particle when needed. Not every Korean sentence needs an object.

notes.title: Consonant vs Vowel
notes.content: Use 을 after consonant-ending nouns (음악을) and 를 after vowel-ending nouns (커피를).

lessonExamples.notes: 커피 ends in vowel → 를.
책 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을.

grammarPoints.title: 에게 / 한테 (to someone)
grammarPoints.hint: These particles mark the person or animal receiving a message, gift or action.
grammarPoints.description: These particles mark the person or animal receiving a message, gift or action. 한테 is common in speech, while 에게 appears frequently in writing.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: Add 에게 or 한테 after the recipient: 친구에게/친구한테. The thing given normally takes 을/를: 친구한테 책을 줘요.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 에게 or 한테 after the recipient: 친구에게/친구한테. The thing given normally takes 을/를: 친구한테 책을 줘요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 친구한테 편지를 써요. — I write a letter to a friend. 친구한테 편지를 써요 marks the friend as the recipient of the letter-writing action.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Place 에 marks locations or destinations, but 한테/에게 usually identify animate recipients. For a respected recipient, learn 께.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I write a letter to a friend.
I give a present to my younger sibling.

cards.englishHint: I send a photo to a friend.
I give water to a child.

grammarPoints.title: 에게서 / 한테서 (from someone)
grammarPoints.hint: When an object or message comes from a person, these particles mark that person as the source.
grammarPoints.description: When an object or message comes from a person, these particles mark that person as the source. They are useful with receiving, hearing and learning.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: Attach 에게서 or 한테서 to the source person: 친구에게서, 친구한테서. The received thing still takes 을/를: 친구한테서 책을 받았어요.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 에게서 or 한테서 to the source person: 친구에게서, 친구한테서. The received thing still takes 을/를: 친구한테서 책을 받았어요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 선생님에게서 편지를 받았어요. — I received a letter from the teacher. 선생님에게서 편지를 받았어요 identifies the teacher as the person the letter came from.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not use 에게서 for the recipient you GIVE something to; use 에게 or 한테. These are common but not interchangeable roles.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I received a letter from the teacher.
I got a photo from a friend.

grammarPoints.title: 안
grammarPoints.description: 안 placed before an action or description usually means 'not'. It often expresses a choice, habit, or simple negation.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Put 안 before the main verb: 안 먹어요, 안 가요. In many noun+하다 verbs, put it between the noun and 해요: 공부 안 해요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 저는 커피를 안 마셔요. — I don't drink coffee. 커피를 안 마셔요: 안 sits directly before 마셔요, so the speaker does not drink coffee.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 안 is different from 못 ('can't'). For 'not a student', use 학생이 아니에요, not 안 학생이에요.

notes.title: 하다 Verbs
notes.content: For noun+하다 verbs, 안 goes between: 공부 안 해요 is the usual spoken placement for 공부하다.

notes.title: 안 vs -지 않다
notes.content: 안 is the short form. The long form -지 않다 is taught later and used in formal/written contexts.

lessonExamples.notes: Uses 은/는 (GP3), 을/를 (GP10), -아요/어요 (GP11).
Uses 은/는 (GP3), -아요/어요 (GP11). 하다 verb split: 공부 안 해요.

grammarPoints.title: -지 않다
grammarPoints.description: -지 않다 is another way to say 'not do' or 'not be' with an action or descriptive verb. It often sounds more measured than short 안.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Remove 다 from the verb, add 지 않다, and conjugate 않다: 먹다 → 먹지 않아요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 저는 고기를 먹지 않아요. — I do not eat meat. 고기를 먹지 않아요: 먹 + 지 않아요 makes the eating negative. The whole expression still ends politely.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: This is not the construction for 'not a doctor' (의사가 아니에요). It does not automatically mean a stronger 'no' than 안.

notes.title: 안 vs -지 않다
notes.content: 안 먹어요 and 먹지 않아요 mean the same thing. -지 않다 can sound a little more formal or measured, but is not automatically stronger.

notes.title: 하다 Verbs
notes.content: For 하다 verbs, -지 않다 is simpler: 공부하지 않아요 (compare: 공부 안 해요).

grammarPoints.title: 못
grammarPoints.description: 못 before a verb means 'cannot' or 'am unable to'. It points to lack of ability or circumstances that prevent the action.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Put 못 before a normal verb: 못 가요, 못 먹어요. With noun+하다, say 공부 못 해요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 저는 매운 음식을 못 먹어요. — I can't eat spicy food. 매운 음식을 못 먹어요: 못 before 먹어요 means the person is unable to eat spicy food.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't use 못 for a deliberate preference when you just mean 'I don't want to'. 안 먹어요 is 'I don't eat'; 못 먹어요 is 'I can't eat'.

notes.title: 못 vs 안
notes.content: 못 = cannot (inability/impossibility). 안 = do not (choice/preference). 못 먹어요 (can't eat) vs 안 먹어요 (don't eat).

notes.title: 하다 Split
notes.content: For Noun+하다 verbs: 공부 못 해요 (cannot study), not 못 공부해요.

grammarPoints.title: -지 못하다 (long-form inability)
grammarPoints.hint: Use -지 못하다 to say someone cannot perform an action because of limited ability or circumstances.
grammarPoints.description: Use -지 못하다 to say someone cannot perform an action because of limited ability or circumstances. It is a longer alternative to 못 + verb.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: Remove 다 from the action verb, attach 지 못하다, then conjugate 못하다: 가다

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Remove 다 from the action verb, attach 지 못하다, then conjugate 못하다: 가다 → 가지 못해요; 먹다 → 먹지 못했어요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 오늘은 학교에 가지 못해요. — I can't go to school today. 오늘은 학교에 가지 못해요 says the speaker is unable to go to school, with 가지 못해요 as the inability construction.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: This is inability, not simply choosing not to act. Compare 가지 않아요 ('don't go') with 가지 못해요 ('can't go').

lessonExamples.englishHint: I can't go to school today.

grammarPoints.title: 여기
grammarPoints.description: 여기 means 'here', near the speaker. It is the place counterpart of 여기/거기/저기.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Use 여기 when naming where you are. Add a correct particle if a full sentence needs one: 여기는, 여기에, 여기에서.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 여기는 학교예요. — Here is a school. 여기는 학교예요 says 'This place is a school'. 는 makes 'here' the topic.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 여기 is a place word, not a general subject pronoun. 여기에서 is for an action occurring here; 여기에 for being or going here.

notes.title: Three-Way Places
notes.content: 여기/거기/저기 follow the same 이/그/저 pattern as 이것/그것/저것.

lessonExamples.notes: Uses 은/는 (GP3), 예요 (GP1).

grammarPoints.title: 거기
grammarPoints.description: 거기 means 'there', often near the listener or at a place already being discussed.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Choose 거기 rather than 여기 when pointing to the other person's place. Then attach a particle: 거기는, 거기에.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 거기는 학교예요? — Is that place a school? 거기는 학교예요? asks whether the place by the listener is a school.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't assume 거기 and 저기 are identical. 저기 normally points to somewhere away from both people.

notes.title: Reference
notes.content: 거기 can also refer to a place already mentioned in the conversation, similar to English "there" or "that place."

grammarPoints.title: 저기
grammarPoints.description: 저기 means 'over there', for a location away from speaker and listener.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Use 저기 for a distant place. Add the particle demanded by the sentence: 저기는, 저기에, 저기에서.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 저기는 공원이에요. — Over there is a park. 저기는 공원이에요: 저기 points to a place far from both speakers. 는 marks that place as the topic, and 공원이에요 identifies it.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 저기 can also be used to get someone's attention; that separate conversational use is not the location pattern practiced here.

notes.title: Attention Getter
notes.content: 저기요! is a common way to get a stranger's attention, like "Excuse me!" at a restaurant.

cards.englishHint: That place over there is also a restaurant.
That place over there is a bank.

grammarPoints.title: 에 (장소)
grammarPoints.description: 에 marks where someone or something is, or the destination of movement: 'at', 'in', or 'to'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Place 에 after the destination/location noun: 학교에, 집에, 방에.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 학교에 가요. — I go to school. 학교에 가요: 학교 is the destination, and 에 marks 'to school'.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: For the place where an activity happens, use 에서: 학교에서 공부해요. English 'at' can translate to either particle.

notes.title: 에 vs 에서
notes.content: 에 marks destination or static location (with 있다). 에서 marks where an action happens (with action verbs like 공부하다).

notes.title: Two Uses
notes.content: Destination: 학교에 가요 (go to school). Static location: 집에 있어요 (am at home).

lessonExamples.notes: The library is the destination. Compare 도서관에서 공부해요, where the library is the place of the action.
에 identifies a motion verb’s destination; existence with 있다 is introduced next.

grammarPoints.title: 에서
grammarPoints.description: 에서 marks the place where an action takes place. Think 'at/in a place, doing something'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Put 에서 after the location noun before an action verb: 도서관에서 공부해요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 도서관에서 공부해요. — I study at the library. 도서관에서 공부해요 means studying happens in the library; 도서관 is not a destination here.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't substitute 에 just because English uses 'at'. 학교에 가요 marks where you go, whereas 학교에서 공부해요 marks where you study.

notes.title: 에서 vs 에
notes.content: Use 에서 for the location of an action (에서 공부해요 = study at). Use 에 for destination or static existence (에 가요 = go to, 에 있어요 = am at).

lessonExamples.englishHint: I drink coffee at the café.
I read a book at the library.
lessonExamples.notes: Reading is the action. The library tells you where it happens.

cards.englishHint: I drink coffee at the café.

grammarPoints.title: 위/아래/앞/뒤/옆
grammarPoints.description: Korean places words such as 위 (above/on), 아래 (below), 앞 (front), 뒤 (behind), and 옆 (beside) after a reference noun.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Say the reference thing first, then the position word, then 에 if saying where something is: 책상 위에.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 책이 책상 위에 있어요. — The book is on the desk. 책이 책상 위에 있어요: 책상 is the reference, 위 means 'above/on it', and 에 locates the book there.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: English often says 'on the desk', but Korean says 'desk + top + at'. Don't reverse the noun and position word.

notes.title: Five Position Words
notes.content: 위 (above/on), 아래 (below/under), 앞 (in front), 뒤 (behind), 옆 (beside/next to).

notes.title: Word Order
notes.content: Reference noun comes first, then the position: 책상 위에 = "desk above-at" = on the desk.

lessonExamples.englishHint: The book is on the desk.
The cat is under the chair.
There is a tree behind the house.
lessonExamples.notes: 집 뒤에 literally puts the house first, then “behind,” then the location particle.

cards.englishHint: The book is on the desk.
The cat is under the chair.
There is a store in front of the school.
There is a café next to the bank.
There is a park behind the school.

grammarPoints.title: 에 (시간)
grammarPoints.description: 에 also marks when something happens, such as a clock time or a specific day.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Find the day or clock time that answers 'when?'. Put 에 immediately after that time: 월요일에, 세 시에, 아침에.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 월요일에 한국어를 공부해요. — I study Korean on Monday. 월요일에 한국어를 공부해요 means studying happens on Monday. 에 gives the time of the action.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't automatically add 에 after every time word: 오늘, 내일, 어제 and 지금 normally stand without it.

notes.title: Not with 오늘/내일/어제
notes.content: 오늘, 내일, 어제, 지금 do NOT take 에 — they are already adverbs of time: ✗ 오늘에, ✓ 오늘.

notes.title: Shared Particle
notes.content: 에 serves both location and time. Context makes it clear.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I go to school at 9 o'clock.

grammarPoints.title: 부터
grammarPoints.description: 부터 marks where a time or range starts: 'from' or 'starting at'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 부터 immediately after the starting time or point: 아홉 시부터.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 9시부터 일해요. — I work from 9. 9시부터 일해요: work starts at 9; 부터 belongs to the starting time.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 부터 gives the beginning, not the end; use 까지 for 'until'. For movement from a place, 에서 is often more natural than 부터.

notes.title: Often Paired
notes.content: 부터 often pairs with 까지: 부터~까지 = "from~until."

notes.title: Time Only
notes.content: 부터 is mainly used for time. For place "from," use 에서.

cards.englishHint: I start studying in the morning.

grammarPoints.title: 까지
grammarPoints.description: 까지 marks the end of a time, range, or destination: 'until', 'up to', or 'as far as'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Choose the finishing time or destination, then add 까지: 여섯 시까지, 학교까지. To name the starting point as well, use 부터 there.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 6시까지 일해요. — I work until 6. 6시까지 일해요: work lasts until six; 까지 points to the cutoff.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't swap 까지 and 부터. A full interval is usually X부터 Y까지 (from X to Y).

notes.title: Time & Place
notes.content: 까지 works for both time (6시까지 "until 6") and place (서울까지 "to Seoul").

lessonExamples.englishHint: I study from morning until evening.

cards.englishHint: I travel from Seoul to Busan.

grammarPoints.title: 전에
grammarPoints.description: 전에 means 'before' when put after a noun or named event.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Put the noun/event first and add 전에: 수업 전에 ('before class'). Verbs need -기 전에, which is introduced later.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 수업 전에 커피를 마셔요. — I drink coffee before class. 수업 전에 커피를 마셔요: 수업 ('class') is the event. Put 전에 after 수업; the coffee-drinking happens before that event.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't attach 전에 directly to a plain verb stem. 먹기 전에 is 'before eating'; 먹전에 is not Korean.

notes.title: Two Patterns
notes.content: With nouns: 수업 전에 (before class). With verbs: 먹기 전에 (before eating) — uses the -기 nominalizer.

grammarPoints.title: 후에
grammarPoints.description: 후에 means 'after' when placed after a noun or named event. It tells the listener which event finishes before the next action.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Put the noun/event first and add 후에: 수업 후에 ('after class'). For a completed verb action, use -(으)ㄴ 후에 later.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 수업 후에 운동해요. — I exercise after class. 수업 후에 운동해요: 수업 is 'class', and 후에 places exercise AFTER that class. No verb ending is needed on the noun 수업.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't use 후에 directly after an unconjugated verb stem. 먹은 후에 is 'after eating', not 먹후에.

notes.title: Synonym
notes.content: 다음에 is a more casual alternative meaning "after" or "next time."

notes.title: Two Patterns
notes.content: With nouns: 수업 후에 (after class). With verbs: 먹은 후에 (after eating).

cards.englishHint: I meet a friend after work.
I take a walk after dinner.

lessons.title: Talking About the Past and Describing Things

grammarPoints.title: -았어요/-었어요
grammarPoints.description: -았어요/-었어요 makes an action or state past in everyday polite speech.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Remove 다. Use 았어요 after most stems with ㅏ/ㅗ, 었어요 after others, and 했어요 for 하다; contractions are common.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 어제 학교에 갔어요. — I went to school yesterday. 가다 → 갔어요. 어제 학교에 갔어요 means 'I went to school yesterday'.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not keep both the old vowel and the new vowel when they contract: 가았어요 is wrong; 갔어요 is correct.

notes.title: Vowel Harmony
notes.content: Last vowel ㅏ/ㅗ → 았어요. Other vowels → 었어요. 하다 → 했어요 (special).

notes.title: Contraction
notes.content: 가 + 았어요 → 갔어요, 보 + 았어요 → 봤어요, 마시 + 었어요 → 마셨어요. The vowels merge.

lessonExamples.notes: 보다 → 봤어요. 보 and 았 combine to make 봤.

grammarPoints.title: ㅅ irregular: 짓다 → 지어요
grammarPoints.hint: Some verbs whose stem ends in ㅅ drop that final consonant before vowel-starting endings.
grammarPoints.description: Some verbs whose stem ends in ㅅ drop that final consonant before vowel-starting endings. The result can look shorter than the dictionary form.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: For selected ㅅ-irregular stems, remove 다 and the final ㅅ before the vowel ending: 짓다

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: For selected ㅅ-irregular stems, remove 다 and the final ㅅ before the vowel ending: 짓다 → 지어요, 낫다 → 나아요. The consonant remains before endings starting with consonants.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 새 집을 지어요. — We build a new house. 짓다 becomes 지어요 because its ㅅ is dropped before -어요, rather than producing 짓어요.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Not every ㅅ-final verb is irregular: 웃다 → 웃어요 and 씻다 → 씻어요. Those verbs retain their ㅅ.

grammarPoints.title: ㅎ irregular: 파랗다 → 파래요
grammarPoints.hint: Some colour and descriptive words ending in ㅎ drop that consonant or change their vowel when they conjugate.
grammarPoints.description: Some colour and descriptive words ending in ㅎ drop that consonant or change their vowel when they conjugate. The form is important for natural descriptions.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: Selected ㅎ-irregular stems change before vowel endings: 파랗다

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Selected ㅎ-irregular stems change before vowel endings: 파랗다 → 파래요, 그렇다 → 그래요, 어떻다 → 어때요. Before a noun, 파랗다 → 파란 하늘.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 하늘이 파래요. — The sky is blue. 하늘이 파래요 uses 파래요 because 파랗다 is an irregular descriptive stem.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 좋다 is a regular ㅎ-final word: 좋아요, 좋은. Do not treat all words written with final ㅎ as irregular.

grammarPoints.title: ㄹ deletion before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ
grammarPoints.hint: Stems ending in ㄹ often lose ㄹ when an ending beginning with ㄴ, ㅂ or ㅅ is added.
grammarPoints.description: Stems ending in ㄹ often lose ㄹ when an ending beginning with ㄴ, ㅂ or ㅅ is added. This is common in formal speech and honorifics.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: When an ending beginning ㄴ, ㅂ or ㅅ follows, remove the stem-final ㄹ: 살다

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: When an ending beginning ㄴ, ㅂ or ㅅ follows, remove the stem-final ㄹ: 살다 → 삽니다, 만들다 → 만드세요, 알다 → 아는 사람.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 저는 서울에 삽니다. — I live in Seoul. 서울에 삽니다 shows that 살다 loses ㄹ before formal -ㅂ니다, so 삽니다 is correct.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not drop ㄹ before every ending: 살아요 keeps it, and 살면 keeps it. Check the initial consonant of the attached ending.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄴ
grammarPoints.description: Descriptive verbs (often called adjectives) can go before a noun using -(으)ㄴ: a 'big bag', 'small cat', or 'good book'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Remove 다 from a descriptive verb. Add 은 after most consonant-ending stems or ㄴ after vowel-ending stems: 작다 → 작은, 크다 → 큰.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 큰 가방이 있어요. — There is a big bag. 큰 가방이 있어요: start with 크다 ('to be big'), remove 다, and add ㄴ to 크 to form 큰. Put 큰 directly before 가방 ('bag').

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: This is not the present modifier of an action verb: 'a person who reads' needs 읽는 사람. ㄹ-final and some irregular stems also change.

notes.title: ㄹ-Irregular
notes.content: If the stem ends in ㄹ, drop ㄹ and add -ㄴ: 길다 → 긴, 멀다 → 먼.

notes.title: Action Verbs Differ
notes.content: Action verbs generally take -는 for present modification. They can take -(으)ㄴ for a completed action. Forms such as 있는 and 없는 also use -는.

cards.englishHint: I live in a small house.

grammarPoints.title: 만
grammarPoints.description: 만 means 'only' or 'just', limiting the person or thing you mean.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 만 directly to the noun or phrase being restricted: 물만, 나만.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 물만 마셔요. — I drink only water. 물만 마셔요: 물 means 'water'. Attach 만 immediately after 물 to limit the drinks to water, rather than saying water is one of several drinks.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't confuse 만 with 도: 물도 means 'water too', but 물만 means 'water and nothing else' in the relevant set.

notes.title: Replaces Markers
notes.content: 만 typically replaces 은/는, 이/가, 을/를. 물을 마셔요 → 물만 마셔요.

notes.title: Stacking
notes.content: 만 can combine with location particles: 집에서만 (only at home), 학교에만 (only to school).

grammarPoints.title: 하고
grammarPoints.description: 하고 can connect nouns: 'A and B' or 'with someone'. It is commonly used in casual conversation.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Name the first noun, add 하고, then name the second: 빵하고 우유. If the pair is an object, put 을/를 on the final noun.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 빵하고 우유를 사요. — I buy bread and milk. 빵하고 우유를 사요 means 'I buy bread and milk'; 를 goes on the whole noun grouping's last word.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't confuse noun-connecting 하고 with action-connecting -고. 먹고 means 'eat and (then)'; 빵하고 means 'bread and'.

notes.title: Formal Alternatives
notes.content: More formal/written: 과 (after consonant) / 와 (after vowel). Casual alternative: (이)랑.

notes.title: No Allomorphs
notes.content: 하고 doesn't change form — it's always 하고 regardless of the preceding syllable.

lessonExamples.notes: Uses 을/를 (GP10), -아요/어요 (GP11).
Uses -아요/어요 (GP11).

grammarPoints.title: 와/과 (and / with nouns)
grammarPoints.hint: 와/과 joins nouns or marks someone you do an action together with.
grammarPoints.description: 와/과 joins nouns or marks someone you do an action together with. It is slightly more common in writing or careful speech than 하고.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: After a noun ending in a vowel add 와, after a consonant add 과: 사과와 바나나, 책과 연필. For doing something together: 친구와 영화 봐요.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: After a noun ending in a vowel add 와, after a consonant add 과: 사과와 바나나, 책과 연필. For doing something together: 친구와 영화 봐요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 사과와 바나나를 샀어요. — I bought apples and bananas. 사과와 바나나를 샀어요 uses 와 to join two object nouns into one list.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: The choice 와 versus 과 depends on the preceding syllable, not the next word. Compare the more conversational 하고 and (이)랑.

cards.englishHint: I go together with a friend.
I bought a bag and shoes.

grammarPoints.title: (이)랑 (and / with)
grammarPoints.hint: (이)랑 is a conversational way to say 'and' or 'with' between nouns or people.
grammarPoints.description: (이)랑 is a conversational way to say 'and' or 'with' between nouns or people. It commonly appears in everyday informal speech.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: Use 이랑 after a final consonant and 랑 after a vowel: 책이랑 공책, 친구랑 영화. The two forms play the same connecting role.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Use 이랑 after a final consonant and 랑 after a vowel: 책이랑 공책, 친구랑 영화. The two forms play the same connecting role.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 친구랑 영화를 봐요. — I watch a movie with my friend. 친구랑 영화를 봐요 means the speaker watches a movie together with a friend.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: For a formal report or academic writing, 와/과 is usually a better choice. Don't attach the consonant form 이랑 after a vowel-ending noun.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I watch a movie with my friend.
I bought a book and a notebook.

cards.englishHint: I play with my younger sibling.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)시-
grammarPoints.description: Use -(으)시- inside a verb to show respect to the PERSON being described, not merely the person listening.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Remove 다, add 시 after a vowel stem or 으시 after most consonant stems, then the ending: 오다 → 오세요, 읽다 → 읽으세요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 선생님이 오세요. — The teacher is coming. 선생님이 오세요 describes the teacher respectfully; 오 + 시 + 어요 contracts to 오세요.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: The same -세요 surface form can also be a polite command. Check who the subject is; do not confuse respect for the subject with polite -요 for the listener.

notes.title: Subject vs listener
notes.content: 선생님이 오세요 describes the teacher respectfully; the -요 polite ending separately addresses the listener.

notes.title: Two readings of -세요
notes.content: 가세요 can be an honorific statement ('[A respected person] goes') or a polite request ('Please go'); context and subject determine which.

notes.title: Stem-final ㄹ
notes.content: Stems ending in ㄹ lose ㄹ before -시-: 살다 → 사세요; 만들다 → 만드세요.

lessonExamples.englishHint: My father is reading a book.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)세요
grammarPoints.description: Use -(으)세요 to politely ask someone to do something: 'please sit', 'please read'. The same form can also describe a respected subject.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Remove 다; after most consonant stems add 으세요, after vowel stems add 세요: 읽다 → 읽으세요, 가다 → 가세요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 여기에 앉으세요. — Please sit here. 여기에 앉으세요 is an instruction to sit here, spoken politely.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: -세요 is not always a command. 선생님이 오세요 is instead an honorific statement; context matters.

notes.title: Dual Use
notes.content: -(으)세요 is both a polite imperative ("please do") and an honorific form. Context determines meaning.

notes.title: Irregular
notes.content: ㄹ-ending stems drop ㄹ: 만들다 → 만드세요. 듣다 → 들으세요 (ㄷ-irregular).

grammarPoints.title: 께서 (honorific subject)
grammarPoints.hint: 께서 is a respectful subject marker used for people the speaker honors.
grammarPoints.description: 께서 is a respectful subject marker used for people the speaker honors. It can replace 이/가 when describing a teacher, elder or another respected person.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: Put 께서 after the respected person's noun or title: 선생님께서, 할머니께서. Use an honorific verb form when appropriate: 선생님께서 오세요.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Put 께서 after the respected person's noun or title: 선생님께서, 할머니께서. Use an honorific verb form when appropriate: 선생님께서 오세요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 선생님께서 오세요. — The teacher is coming (respectfully). 선생님께서 들어오세요 uses 께서 to honor the subject and -시- in 들어오세요 to honor the action's performer.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 께서 is a SUBJECT marker. It is not the same as 께, which marks a respected recipient, or ordinary 이/가.

cards.englishHint: The teacher is reading a book.

grammarPoints.title: 께 (to a respected person)
grammarPoints.hint: 께 is a respectful alternative to 에게/한테 when someone important to the speaker receives a gift, message or action.
grammarPoints.description: 께 is a respectful alternative to 에게/한테 when someone important to the speaker receives a gift, message or action.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: Put 께 after the recipient's name or title: 선생님께, 할머니께. Keep the object separately marked: 선생님께 편지를 드려요.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Put 께 after the recipient's name or title: 선생님께, 할머니께. Keep the object separately marked: 선생님께 편지를 드려요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 선생님께 편지를 드려요. — I give the teacher a letter (respectfully). 선생님께 편지를 드려요 marks the teacher as the respected recipient of the letter.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 께 marks the person receiving something; 께서 instead marks the respected subject doing the action. Do not confuse the two.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I give the teacher a letter (respectfully).

cards.englishHint: I ask the professor a question (respectfully).

grammarPoints.title: -아/어 주세요
grammarPoints.description: Use -아/어 주세요 to ask someone politely to do an action as a favor.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 아/어 to the action stem, then write 주세요 as a separate word: 찍다 → 찍어 주세요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 사진을 찍어 주세요. — Please take a photo (for me). 사진을 찍어 주세요: 'Please take a photo (for me).' The request asks for the action as a favor.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: -아/어 주세요 is not simply another way to make every imperative. It specifically asks someone to do something for someone else's benefit.

notes.title: -(으)세요 vs -아/어 주세요
notes.content: -(으)세요 is a general polite command. -아/어 주세요 specifically asks "please do this for me" — implies a favor.

notes.title: Common Phrases
notes.content: 도와주세요 (please help), 알려 주세요 (please let me know), 기다려 주세요 (please wait).

grammarPoints.title: -아/어야 하다
grammarPoints.description: Use -아/어야 하다 to say something is necessary: 'must' or 'have to'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: After the verb stem add 아야/어야, followed by 해요: 가다 → 가야 해요, 먹다 → 먹어야 해요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 내일 학교에 가야 해요. — I have to go to school tomorrow. 내일 학교에 가야 해요: 가야 says going is required; 해요 completes the obligation.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 'Must not' is NOT -아/어야 안 하다. Use -(으)면 안 되다 or -지 마세요 for prohibitions.

notes.title: Vowel Harmony
notes.content: Same as -아요/어요: stem ㅏ/ㅗ → 아야 해요; otherwise → 어야 해요. 하다 → 해야 해요.

notes.title: Negative
notes.content: -지 않아도 돼요 means "don't have to" (no obligation). Not covered here but useful to know.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I have to go to school tomorrow.

cards.englishHint: I have to go to school tomorrow.

grammarPoints.title: -고 싶다
grammarPoints.description: Use -고 싶다 to say what you want to do, or ask what the listener wants.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 고 to the action stem and conjugate 싶다: 가다 → 가고 싶어요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 한국에 가고 싶어요. — I want to go to Korea. 한국에 가고 싶어요: the speaker wants to go to Korea, not that the trip is already planned.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: For a third person's desire, Korean commonly uses -고 싶어하다, not plain -고 싶다 in a declarative statement.

notes.title: First/Second Person
notes.content: -고 싶다 is for "I want" or "Do you want?" For third person desires, use -고 싶어하다.

notes.title: No Conjugation Needed
notes.content: The verb stem stays unchanged: 가다 → 가고 싶어요, 먹다 → 먹고 싶어요. No vowel harmony rules.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I want to go to Korea.

cards.englishHint: I want to go to Korea.
I want to watch a movie.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄹ 수 있다
grammarPoints.hint: can, able to / cannot, unable to
grammarPoints.description: Use -(으)ㄹ 수 있다 to say an action is possible or someone has the ability to do it.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 을 to most consonant-ending verb stems or ㄹ to vowel-ending stems, then 수 있어요: 읽다 → 읽을 수 있어요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 한국어를 읽을 수 있어요. — I can read Korean. 한국어를 읽을 수 있어요: 읽을 수 is the ability to read, and 있어요 says that ability exists.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Keep 수 as a separate word. 못 읽어요 can express inability too, but does not have the same grammatical structure.

notes.title: Allomorphs
notes.content: Consonant stem: 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. Vowel stem: 가다 → 갈 수 있어요. ㄹ stem: 만들다 → 만들 수 있어요 (ㄹ stays).

notes.title: 있다 vs 없다
notes.content: 수 있다 = can/able. 수 없다 = cannot/unable. Both conjugate normally: 있어요/없어요.

lessonExamples.notes: 없어요 gives the negative meaning. 수 is separated from the verb by a space.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)니까
grammarPoints.description: Use -(으)니까 to explain a reason, often before telling someone what to do or suggesting an action.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 으니까 after most consonant stems or 니까 after vowel stems: 없다 → 없으니까.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 시간이 없으니까 빨리 가세요. — Please go quickly because there's no time. 시간이 없으니까 빨리 가세요: 'Since there's no time, please go quickly.' The reason supports an instruction.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Unlike causal -아/어서 in the beginner pattern, -(으)니까 naturally works before an imperative or suggestion. Past marking is also possible.

notes.title: -(으)니까 vs -아/어서
notes.content: -(으)니까 is more subjective and can precede commands: 시간이 없으니까 빨리 가세요. Use -(으)니까 for a reason followed by a command or suggestion in this lesson.

notes.title: Past OK
notes.content: -(으)니까 allows past tense: 이미 먹었으니까 안 먹어요 (I already ate, so I'm not eating).

lessonExamples.englishHint: Please go quickly because there's no time.
Please dress warmly because it's cold.

cards.englishHint: Please go quickly because there's no time.
Take an umbrella because it's raining.
Please eat a lot because it's delicious.

grammarPoints.title: -아/어서
grammarPoints.description: Use -아/어서 to connect a cause with its result: 'because X, Y'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 아서 after ㅏ/ㅗ stems, 어서 after others; 하다 → 해서. Put tense on the main verb in these beginner examples.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 배가 고파서 밥을 먹었어요. — I ate because I was hungry. 배가 고파서 밥을 먹었어요: being hungry explains eating; only the final verb marks past here.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not use causal -아/어서 before a direct command in the standard beginner pattern. Use -(으)니까 for that reason→command relationship.

notes.title: Where to put tense
notes.content: For these beginner examples, leave the reason clause unmarked for tense and mark the main verb. Compare -(으)니까 when explicitly marking a past reason.

notes.title: Common Combinations
notes.content: 만나서 반갑습니다 (Nice to meet you — lit. "meeting, I am pleased"). 늦어서 죄송합니다 (Sorry for being late).

lessonExamples.englishHint: I ate because I was hungry.
I stayed home because I was tired.

cards.englishHint: I ate because I was hungry.
I took an umbrella because it was raining.
I took a taxi because I was late.

grammarPoints.title: 그래서
grammarPoints.description: 그래서 begins a new sentence with the result: 'so' or 'therefore'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Say the reason as a finished sentence; start the next sentence with 그래서.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 배가 고팠어요. 그래서 밥을 먹었어요. — I was hungry. So I ate. 배가 고팠어요. 그래서 밥을 먹었어요: hunger is one sentence, eating is the consequence.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 그래서 joins sentences, not verb stems. Don't attach it as a suffix like -아/어서.

notes.title: Sentence Connector
notes.content: 그래서 connects two independent sentences. Unlike -아/어서 and -(으)니까, it doesn't connect clauses within one sentence.

notes.title: Related Words
notes.content: 그래서 (so/therefore), 그런데 (but/however), 그리고 (and/also) are the three most common sentence connectors.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I was hungry. So I ate.
It rained. So I stayed home.

cards.englishHint: I was hungry. So I ate.
I had no time. So I took a taxi.
I like Korean. So I study every day.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)면
grammarPoints.description: Use -(으)면 to say 'if' or 'when' one condition makes another possible.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 으면 after most consonant-ending verb stems and 면 after vowel-ending stems: 있다 → 있으면.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 시간이 있으면 같이 가요. — If you have time, let's go together. 시간이 있으면 같이 가요: start with 있다 ('to have'), add 으면 to get 있으면 ('if there is'). Going together depends on having time.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: A final ㄹ stays: 살다 → 살면, not 사으면. For a mere reason ('because'), choose a reason connective instead.

notes.title: Hypothetical & Habitual
notes.content: -(으)면 covers both hypothetical (if it rains) and habitual (whenever I eat). Context determines which.

notes.title: ㄹ-Irregular
notes.content: Stems ending in ㄹ keep ㄹ before -면: 살다 → 살면, 알다 → 알면.

lessonExamples.englishHint: If you have time, let's go together.
If it rains, I stay home.

cards.englishHint: If you have time, let's go together.
If I go to Korea, I want to eat bulgogi.
If the weather is nice, I go to the park.

grammarPoints.title: -지만
grammarPoints.description: -지만 joins two facts that contrast, meaning 'but'. One fact remains true even though another might make you expect the opposite.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 지만 directly to the stem of a verb or descriptive verb; no vowel-choice rule: 비싸다 → 비싸지만.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 비싸지만 맛있어요. — It's expensive but it's delicious. 비싸지만 맛있어요: it is expensive but tasty; the two facts contrast.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not confuse -지만 (inside one sentence) with 하지만 (at the start of a second sentence).

notes.title: No Vowel Harmony
notes.content: -지만 attaches directly to any stem. No consonant/vowel distinction. 먹다 → 먹지만, 가다 → 가지만.

notes.title: With Tense
notes.content: Past: 갔지만, 먹었지만. The tense goes between the stem and -지만.

cards.englishHint: I'm tired but I have to study.
It's small but a nice house.

grammarPoints.title: 하지만
grammarPoints.description: 하지만 starts a new sentence meaning 'but' or 'however'. It contrasts with what was just said.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Finish the first sentence. Begin the next with 하지만 and give the unexpected or opposing fact.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 한국어는 어려워요. 하지만 재미있어요. — Korean is hard. But it's fun. 한국어는 어려워요. 하지만 재미있어요: Korean is hard; however, it is fun.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't glue 하지만 onto a verb stem. For two clauses in one sentence use -지만: 어렵지만 재미있어요.

notes.title: -지만 vs 하지만
notes.content: -지만 connects clauses within one sentence. 하지만 connects two separate sentences. Same meaning, different scope.

notes.title: Similar Words
notes.content: 하지만, 그런데, 그렇지만 all mean "but/however." 하지만 is the most common in writing.

lessonExamples.englishHint: Korean is hard. But it's fun.
It rained. But I went to the park.

cards.englishHint: Korean is hard. But it's fun.
That restaurant is expensive. But it's delicious.
I'm tired. But I have to study.

grammarPoints.title: -고
grammarPoints.description: -고 links actions or lists them: 'do A and do B'. Sometimes the order is sequential, sometimes it just joins facts.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 고 to the first verb stem, then write the next verb phrase: 먹다 → 먹고.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 아침을 먹고 학교에 가요. — I eat breakfast and then go to school. 아침을 먹고 학교에 가요: breakfast comes first, then going to school.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: -고 does not always mean 'and then'. When two actions must be strictly sequential, -고 나서 makes the order clearer.

notes.title: No Conjugation
notes.content: -고 attaches directly to any verb stem. No consonant/vowel rules: 먹고, 가고, 하고. Same form as 하고 (and/with) for nouns.

notes.title: Order Matters
notes.content: When sequential: 손을 씻고 밥을 먹어요 (wash hands THEN eat). When listing: 노래하고 춤을 춰요 (sing and dance, with no fixed time order).

lessonExamples.englishHint: I eat breakfast and then go to school.
I do homework and then watch TV.

cards.englishHint: I eat breakfast and then go to school.
I showered and then got dressed.
I drink coffee and then start work.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄹ게요
grammarPoints.description: Use -(으)ㄹ게요 when the SPEAKER is committing to doing something, often considering the listener.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: After a consonant stem add 을게요; after a vowel stem add ㄹ게요: 하다 → 할게요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 제가 할게요. — I'll do it. 제가 할게요: 하다 becomes 할게요. The speaker volunteers to do the action and signals that promise to the listener.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't use -(으)ㄹ게요 for a neutral prediction about someone else. -(으)ㄹ 거예요 is used for plans or predictions.

notes.title: First Person Only
notes.content: -(으)ㄹ게요 normally expresses the speaker’s own promise, not a prediction about someone else. For other people’s plans, use -(으)ㄹ 거예요.

notes.title: vs -(으)ㄹ 거예요
notes.content: -(으)ㄹ게요 = promise/consideration for listener. -(으)ㄹ 거예요 = plan/prediction (any person).

lessonExamples.englishHint: Is your luggage heavy? I’ll carry it for you.
lessonExamples.notes: The speaker offers to do something for the listener.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄹ 거예요
grammarPoints.description: Use -(으)ㄹ 거예요 for a future plan or prediction: 'will', 'going to', 'probably'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Use 을 after most consonant stems or ㄹ after vowel stems, then write 거예요 separately: 가다 → 갈 거예요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 내일 한국어를 공부할 거예요. — I'm going to study Korean tomorrow. 내일 한국어를 공부할 거예요: 공부하다 becomes 공부할. Add 거예요 separately to express the speaker's future study plan.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Keep 거예요 as a separate word. Compare 제가 할게요 (commitment) with 제가 할 거예요 (plan).

notes.title: All Persons
notes.content: 저는 갈 거예요 (I will go). 친구는 갈 거예요 (My friend will go). 비가 올 거예요 (It will rain). Any subject works.

notes.title: Questions
notes.content: 뭐 할 거예요? (What will you do?), 어디 갈 거예요? (Where will you go?) — very common question patterns.

cards.englishHint: I'm going to study Korean tomorrow.

grammarPoints.title: -네요
grammarPoints.description: -네요 shows the speaker has just noticed or reacted to something: 'Oh, it's...'

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Take off 다 from the dictionary form and add 네요: 좋다 → 좋네요. Use this ending when reacting to something you have noticed.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 날씨가 좋네요. — Oh, the weather is nice! 날씨가 좋네요: the speaker notices and reacts to the pleasant weather.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: -네요 is not just a normal fact-reporting -아요/어요 ending; it carries a feeling of discovery or reaction.

notes.title: Direct Attachment
notes.content: -네요 attaches directly to the verb stem with no modification: 먹다 → 먹네요, 크다 → 크네요.

notes.title: Feeling
notes.content: -네요 conveys "Oh, I see!" or "Oh, how nice!" — a warm, observational tone.

lessonExamples.notes: Uses 이/가 (GP9). Stem 좋 + 네요.
Uses 이것 (GP4), 은/는 (GP3). Stem 맛있 + 네요.

grammarPoints.title: -지요/죠
grammarPoints.description: -지요/죠 often asks for agreement or checks something the speaker thinks the listener knows: 'right?'

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 지요 to a stem; in speech it commonly contracts to 죠: 재미있다 → 재미있지요?

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 한국어는 재미있지요? — Korean is fun, right? 한국어는 재미있지요? checks or invites agreement that Korean is interesting.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't use -지요 for every neutral question. It often implies an expectation that the statement is true.

notes.title: Contraction
notes.content: 지요 → 죠 in casual speech. Both are polite. 죠 is overwhelmingly more common in conversation.

notes.title: Usage
notes.content: Use when you believe the listener already knows or agrees: "한국 음식 좋아하죠?" = "You like Korean food, right?"

lessonExamples.notes: Uses 은/는 (GP3). Stem 재미있 + 지요.
Uses 이것 (GP4), 은/는 (GP3). Contracted form 죠.

grammarPoints.title: -ㄴ 것 같다
grammarPoints.description: -(으)ㄴ 것 같다 softens a judgment about a PRESENT state: 'seems', 'looks like', or 'I think'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Use a descriptive verb's -(으)ㄴ modifier before 것 같아요: 비싸다 → 비싼 것 같아요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 이 음식은 비싼 것 같아요. — This food seems expensive. 이 음식은 비싼 것 같아요: the speaker believes the food seems expensive, rather than stating it as certain.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Action-verb predictions usually use -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요, not this present descriptive-verb pattern. 것 is a separate word.

notes.title: Soft Opinion
notes.content: Korean speakers often use -ㄴ 것 같다 for politeness even when they are sure, to soften the statement.

notes.title: Tense Matters
notes.content: For past: -ㄴ 것 같다 (same form for adj). For action verbs in present: -는 것 같다 (different ending, later lesson).

cards.fullSentence: 그 사람은 한국 사람인 것 같아요.
